subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
title: Uterine Artery and Ureter, Ovarian Drainage and Pelvic Floor

steps.tx: The ureter passes beneath the uterine artery near the cervix, remembered as water under the bridge, the **uterine artery ureter relation**. It is the commonest site of ureteric injury in hysterectomy. Identifying the ureter before clamping the artery prevents it. Careful history taking and examination help place this finding in the right clinical context before treatment is planned.
steps.say: The ureter passes under the uterine artery, the commonest hysterectomy injury site.

vis.alt: Ureter and uterine artery in radical surgery.
vis.caption: Ureter relation. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Ovarian lymph drains along the ovarian vessels to para aortic nodes at renal level, termed **ovarian lymphatic drainage**. This is why ovarian cancer staging samples high para aortic nodes. Uterine drainage goes instead to pelvic node groups. Correlating this finding with imaging and laboratory results prevents both delayed treatment and unnecessary intervention in most patients.
steps.say: Ovarian lymphatic drainage reaches para aortic nodes at renal level along its vessels.

steps.tx: The muscular and fascial diaphragm closing the pelvic outlet is the **pelvic floor**. Levator ani and coccygeus with their fascia support bladder, uterus and rectum against abdominal pressure. Childbirth injury here is the root of later prolapse. Early recognition matters because timely treatment gives clearly better outcomes than waiting for complications to develop first.
steps.say: The pelvic floor diaphragm supports pelvic organs against abdominal pressure.

steps.tx: The uterine artery arises from the internal iliac and reaches the uterus at internal os level, called the **uterine artery course**. It anastomoses freely with ovarian and vaginal branches. This collateral web explains pelvic embolisation safety. Students should connect this fact with the presenting symptoms, since examination questions usually test that clinical link directly.
steps.say: The uterine artery course anastomoses with ovarian and vaginal branches freely.

steps.tx: The ureter enters the pelvis crossing the common iliac bifurcation, a landmark of the **pelvic ureter course**. It then runs medial to the internal iliac under the uterine artery tunnel. Surgeons recite this course before every pelvic operation. Documenting this finding clearly in the notes guides the next clinician and supports safe, well planned further management.
steps.say: The pelvic ureter crosses the iliac bifurcation then passes under the uterine artery.

steps.tx: Ovarian vessels travel in the suspensory ligament and anastomose at the cornu, forming the **ovarian vascular pedicle**. Unrecognised bleeding here retracts into the retroperitoneum silently. Methodical pedicle control prevents broad ligament haematomas. When this picture is seen in practice, urgent senior review is wise whenever there is any doubt about severity.
steps.say: The ovarian vascular pedicle retracts and bleeds retroperitoneally if uncontrolled.

steps.tx: Supports of the uterus rank from levator tone to cardinal and uterosacral ligaments as the **three tier support** system. DeLancey levels describe apical, mid vaginal and distal support for prolapse surgery. Failure at each level produces distinct prolapses. Understanding this mechanism explains the symptoms, the investigation findings and the logic behind each step of treatment given.
steps.say: Three tier support by DeLancey levels explains distinct prolapse types by failure level.

steps.tx: The pudendal nerve through Alcock canal supplies the perineum and is blocked for outlet procedures by the **pudendal block**. Bilateral transvaginal injection at the ischial spine anaesthetises the lower vagina. It serves forceps deliveries and perineal repair. This distinction changes management, so it should be settled early rather than after empirical treatment has already begun.
steps.say: Pudendal block at the ischial spine anaesthetises the perineum for outlet procedures.

steps.tx: Preserving ureteric safety uses visualisation, palpation of vermiculation and sometimes stents, grouped as **ureter protection strategies**. Lighted stents and fluorescence imaging are modern adjuncts in difficult cases. None replaces knowing the anatomy cold. Careful history taking and examination help place this finding in the right clinical context before treatment is planned.
steps.say: Ureter protection strategies assist but never replace knowing the anatomy cold.
